Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette:
Kofi is a 77-year-old Ghanaian-born man who came to the United States as a refugee decades ago following a period of severe political persecution in his home country. He is married, lives with his wife in a quiet suburban neighborhood, and has spent the latter part of his professional life working as a software engineer - a career he built painstakingly after resettlement, teaching himself to code in his forties as a way of constructing a new life from nothing. He was referred for psychological assessment after his wife contacted their family physician, concerned that her husband had become increasingly withdrawn and was rarely leaving the house.

The events that brought Kofi to America began when he was detained by government security forces in his late thirties. He was held for several weeks in a facility where he was subjected to repeated interrogations - men in uniform standing over him, issuing commands in clipped, authoritative voices, demanding answers, demanding compliance, demanding silence. He recalls the guards barking orders as the most viscerally terrifying aspect of the experience: the way a voice raised in command could make the walls of the room feel as though they were closing inward. He eventually escaped through a network of aid workers and spent months moving through transit countries before arriving in the United States. For many years afterward, he managed. He worked. He raised children. He told himself the past was behind him.

What Kofi describes now, however, is a world that has quietly become saturated with threat. When his supervisor at his remote engineering job sends terse, directive messages - "Kofi, I need this completed by end of day" - he finds himself frozen at his keyboard, his chest tight, something in the phrasing pulling him back to a concrete room and a voice that expected obedience or punishment. These moments of being given orders or instructions, however routine in any workplace, have become potent enough that he has begun avoiding video calls entirely, and has requested all communication be asynchronous. Trauma-related news - anything about political detainees, refugee crises, authoritarian governments - acts as a similar lever, and he has removed most news applications from his devices. More unsettling still are the moments when he begins to feel detached or unreal, a dissociative quality that descends without warning and that he experiences as a signal that something worse is coming. These triggers, taken together, have steadily narrowed his world.

Over the past two years, Kofi has stopped going out with any regularity. What began as reluctance to attend crowded places has condensed into a near-total avoidance of leaving the house, and he has also pulled back from social contact, declining invitations from his adult children and deflecting his wife's efforts to bring friends around. To manage the interior pressure of his days, he keeps his mind occupied constantly - coding problems, online chess, documentary series - anything that fills the cognitive space before something unwanted can surface. Yet this relentless mental distraction has an unintended consequence: it keeps his processing of the past shallow and fragmented, so that when memories do break through, they arrive not as coherent narrative but as discrete, frozen images. He describes his memories of the detention as a series of snapshots - a guard's hand on a table, the particular grey of a wall, the angle of light through a small window - each one a still picture, unconnected to what came before or after. Sometimes he can recall these images and feel absolutely nothing, as though reviewing photographs of someone else's life, numb and distant. This emotionless recall unsettles him in its own way; he wonders whether he is damaged beyond ordinary feeling.

The fragmented, image-based nature of these memories means they are poorly anchored in time and context, and so almost anything - a directive tone, a news headline, a moment of unreality - can activate them, sending him back into vigilance. And the more vigilant he becomes, the more he avoids; the more he avoids, the less his memories are ever processed or placed safely in the past; the less they are processed, the more readily a stray trigger can pull one loose.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was his wife telling him quietly one evening that she felt she had lost him. He is most afraid, he says, that she is right.
